candidates.text: Apollo 13 lost an oxygen tank 200,000 miles from Earth.
In seconds, Apollo 13 lost most of its power and oxygen.
Two hundred thousand miles from Earth, an oxygen tank exploded.
So how did a tank that passed every test just explode?
It started with switches rated 28 V. It ended with tank ruptures — mission aborted.
Its heater switches were rated for 28 volts, not 65.
It took only heater switches rated for 28 V run on 65 V.
After Apollo 13, every component rating is now checked against every power source it will ever see, including ground equipment.

paragraphs.text: Apollo 13 lost an oxygen tank 200,000 miles from Earth.
But that was only the visible part. Apollo 13 lost an oxygen tank 200,000 miles from Earth. The key figure: 28 V vs 65 V.

To see why, look at the structure itself. Mar 1970: Pad detanking: heaters run ~8 hours, switches weld shut. Apr 11: Launch. Apr 13, ~56 h in: Tank stir; oxygen tank 2 ruptures. Apr 17: Crew splashes down safely. Two hundred thousand miles from Earth, an oxygen tank exploded. In seconds, Apollo 13 lost most of its power and oxygen. So how did a tank that passed every test just explode? Its heater switches were rated for 28 volts, not 65. They welded shut, and wires inside cooked at a thousand degrees. Weeks later, in space, damaged wiring sparked inside pure oxygen. The crew survived using the lunar module as a lifeboat. One mismatched voltage nearly cost three lives.
And the warning signs were already there. The mechanism: thermostat switches welded shut by overvoltage, overheating the tank's wiring insulation.

Then the chain began. The trigger: heater switches rated for 28 V run on 65 V. Nothing hit Apollo 13. The failure was built in on the ground weeks earlier, when a mismatch in voltage ratings silently damaged the tank.

This is the moment it could no longer be stopped. Step 1 of the failure chain: switches rated 28 V, ground supply 65 V. Step 2 of the failure chain: switches weld shut during detanking. Step 3 of the failure chain: heater cooks wire insulation. Step 4 of the failure chain: spark in pure oxygen in flight. Step 5 of the failure chain: tank ruptures — mission aborted.
Which leaves one question. What changed: every component rating is now checked against every power source it will ever see, including ground equipment.
But that was only the visible part. The switches passed their own tests; the mismatch lived between two teams' specs. Who should own a failure that belongs to no single part?

miniNarrative: The mechanism: thermostat switches welded shut by overvoltage, overheating the tank's wiring insulation.
Kennedy challenged his nation to land an astronaut on the Moon by the end of the decade, with a safe return to Earth.
NASA worked towards this goal incrementally, sending astronauts into space during Project Mercury and Project Gemini, leading up to the Apollo program.
The goal was achieved with Apollo 11, which landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969.
shorts.payoff: There was a greater role for science on Apollo 13, especially for geology, something emphasized by the mission's motto, Ex luna, scientia (From the Moon, knowledge).

miniNarrative: Apollo 13's mission commander, Jim Lovell, was 42 years old at the time of the spaceflight.
At the time of Apollo 13, Lovell was the NASA astronaut with the most time in space, with 572 hours over the three missions.
Fred Haise, the Lunar Module pilot (LMP), was 36 years old.
He held a B.S. in aeronautical engineering, had been a Marine Corps fighter pilot, and was a civilian research pilot for NASA when he was selected as a Group 5 astronaut.
shorts.payoff: Some of this photography was to be performed by Swigert as Lovell and Haise walked on the Moon.
